q: Mr. Reyes steps on a rusty nail. Ten days later his jaw muscles lock and his back arches in sustained spasms. A student says, "That's tetanus, just like the lab trace." What is the key difference between his disease and physiological tetanus?
options: His muscle fibers have lost their calcium pumps
A toxin removes spinal inhibition of motor neurons
His muscles are in a single twitch that never ends
His muscles have lost all of the motor neurons that supply them

q: What does the enzyme creatine kinase do in a working muscle fiber?
options: Splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytosol
Moves phosphate from creatine phosphate to ADP
Pumps calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Binds oxygen and releases it to the mitochondria

q: A sprinter explodes out of the blocks. During the first 5 seconds, where does most of the ATP his leg muscles spend come from?
options: Aerobic respiration of fatty acids
Anaerobic glycolysis of glucose from the blood
Stored ATP and creatine phosphate
Lactate taken up from the blood

q: A kilogram of muscle holds 5 mmol of ATP and 20 mmol of creatine phosphate, and during an all-out effort it spends 2.5 mmol of ATP per second. Ignoring glycolysis and aerobic respiration, how long could stored ATP plus creatine phosphate supply it?
options: 2 seconds
8 seconds
10 seconds
62.5 seconds

q: A fiber needs 90 ATP. Taking 2 ATP per glucose for anaerobic glycolysis and 30 per glucose for aerobic respiration, how many glucose molecules does each route use?
options: Anaerobic 45, aerobic 3
Anaerobic 3, aerobic 45
Anaerobic 180, aerobic 2,700
Anaerobic 30, aerobic 2

q: A student runs 400 meters as fast as she can, which takes about a minute. Predict the change in each variable in her leg muscles at the end of the run, compared with rest.
In the middle panel, pyruvate from glycolysis can take two routes. In a hard-working muscle fiber, what sends pyruvate to become lactate?
options: Glycolysis making pyruvate faster than the mitochondria can take it in
The fiber having run completely out of ATP
Creatine kinase converting pyruvate to lactate
A lack of glucose entering from the blood

fig.alt: A three-panel diagram of how muscle remakes ATP. Top panel: in resting muscle, ATP and creatine combine to form creatine phosphate and ADP; in active muscle, the enzyme creatine kinase moves the phosphate from creatine phosphate back to ADP, giving creatine and ATP for contraction. Middle panel: glucose from the blood and from muscle glycogen enters glycolysis, which yields 2 ATP and 2 pyruvate; with oxygen, pyruvate goes on to aerobic respiration, and without it, it leaves as lactic acid to the blood. Bottom panel: glucose from the blood, pyruvic acid and fatty acids enter a mitochondrion, which uses oxygen to make many ATP, heat, carbon dioxide and water.

q: Thirty seconds into an all-out cycling sprint, which statement best describes the rider's leg muscles?
options: Glycolysis has replaced creatine phosphate, which has switched off
Aerobic respiration has taken over now that the start is over
Creatine phosphate is still supplying nearly all the ATP
All three run; glycolysis supplies the most
misconception: energy systems switch on one after another

q: A biology student notes that a seal's swimming muscles look almost black, and a chicken's leg meat is darker than its breast meat. What best explains the dark color in both?
options: They contain more glycogen
They contain more creatine phosphate
They contain more lactate
They contain more myoglobin

q: Myoglobin binds oxygen more tightly than the oxygen carrier in red blood cells does. What is the effect of this in a muscle fiber?
options: It pulls oxygen from the blood and keeps it until oxygen in the fiber falls very low
It stops the mitochondria from ever running short of oxygen
It makes the fiber less able to take up oxygen from the blood
It lets the fiber make ATP without mitochondria

q: Even in severe muscle fatigue, ATP inside the fibers stays near three quarters of its resting level. Why is it important that ATP does not run out?
options: Without ATP, the fibers would relax completely and become floppy
Without ATP, glycolysis would speed up and flood the fiber with lactate
Without ATP, the fiber would release more calcium from its SR
Without ATP, myosin heads could not detach from actin

q: At about mile 20 of a marathon, a runner who has eaten nothing during the race suddenly slows sharply and says her legs feel empty. What is the most likely cause?
options: Her creatine phosphate stores have just run out
Her leg muscles' glycogen stores are nearly used up
Lactic acid has poisoned her muscles
Her muscle fibers have run completely out of ATP

q: Two days after his first long downhill hike, Mr. Park's thigh muscles are sore and tender. A friend says it is lactic acid left in his muscles. What is the better explanation?
options: Lactate has crystallized in the muscle fibers
His muscles have run out of creatine phosphate
Small fiber injuries from eccentric work
Myoglobin has leaked out of his damaged muscle fibers
misconception: lactic acid causes next-day muscle soreness

q: After a hard 5-minute run, you keep breathing heavily while you stand still. Select everything this excess post-exercise oxygen consumption pays for.
options: Rebuilding creatine phosphate and ATP
Reloading myoglobin with oxygen
Storing extra oxygen for the next run
Clearing lactate by burning it or turning it into glucose
The higher costs of a warmer body and raised hormone levels

q: Put these events in order for a fiber working so hard that it makes lactate.
options: Glycogen in the fiber is broken down to glucose units
Glycolysis splits each glucose into two pyruvate, making ATP and NADH
Pyruvate is produced faster than the mitochondria can take it in
Pyruvate is converted to lactate, regenerating NAD+
Lactate leaves the fiber and is burned by other tissues or made into glucose by the liver

q: A student described the creatine phosphate system. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: At rest, ATP from the mitochondria is used to make creatine phosphate
At the start of hard effort, ADP builds up beside the myosin heads
Creatine kinase uses oxygen to move phosphate onto ADP
Creatine phosphate supplies most new ATP for about 10 seconds

q: Complete the reaction catalyzed by creatine kinase: creatine phosphate + ADP → creatine + ____.
options: ATP
Lactate
Pyruvate
Glucose

q: A man is freed after his legs were pinned under rubble for six hours. Later his urine is dark, tea-colored. Which muscle protein is most likely responsible?
options: Actin
Myoglobin
Creatine kinase
Troponin

q: Twenty minutes into a steady, comfortable bike ride, how are the rider's leg muscles mainly making ATP?
options: Aerobic respiration of fatty acids and glucose in mitochondria
Anaerobic glycolysis of muscle glycogen
Creatine phosphate rebuilt between pedal strokes
Stored ATP from before the ride

q: During a series of hard, repeated contractions, which change inside the fibers is best supported as a major cause of the falling force?
options: Lactate poisoning the myosin heads
ATP falling to zero
Inorganic phosphate building up
Myoglobin running out of iron

q: A student sprints up four flights of stairs and then sits down. Predict how each variable changes over her first 10 minutes of rest, compared with the moment she stops.

variables.name: Creatine phosphate in her leg muscles

q: Which fiber type contracts slowly, is rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, and resists fatigue for hours?
options: Fast glycolytic
Fast oxidative
Slow oxidative
Smooth muscle fiber

q: A sports scientist takes thigh muscle biopsies from an elite marathon runner. Which result would you expect?
options: Mostly fast glycolytic fibers with large glycogen stores
Mostly slow oxidative fibers with many capillaries and mitochondria
Equal numbers of the three types, all pale in color
Fibers much thicker than in untrained people

q: In a biopsy, a technician counts 90 slow oxidative, 70 fast oxidative and 40 fast glycolytic fibers. What percentage of the fibers are slow-twitch?
Why do fast glycolytic fibers fatigue within a minute or two of hard work?
options: Their myosin cannot split ATP
They have no sarcoplasmic reticulum
They burn glycogen fast and build up phosphate
Their motor neurons fire too slowly to keep the fibers contracting

q: Slow oxidative fibers are thinner than fast glycolytic fibers. How does their small diameter suit their metabolism?
options: A thin fiber holds more glycogen per unit of its volume
A thin fiber contracts faster than a thick one
Oxygen has less distance to diffuse
A thin fiber needs no myoglobin

q: A runner who has been running at marathon pace starts an all-out sprint for the finish line. Predict the change in each variable in her leg muscles during the sprint.

variables.name: Share of ATP from aerobic respiration
How long she can keep this pace

q: A previously inactive adult completes eight weeks of regular endurance running. Predict the change in each variable in his leg muscles.

variables.name: Total number of fibers in the muscle

q: Select every change that endurance training produces in skeletal muscle.
options: More capillaries around each fiber
More mitochondria in each fiber
Many new fibers formed by division
More myoglobin
Large increase in fiber diameter
Fast glycolytic fibers taking on fast oxidative properties

q: After a year of heavy weight training, Ms. Tran's thigh muscles are much larger. What mainly accounts for the growth?
options: Existing fibers dividing into two
Existing fibers adding myofibrils
Fat building up between the fibers
Tendons lengthening to make room for more fibers
misconception: muscles grow by adding new fibers

q: During pregnancy the uterus wall thickens partly because its smooth muscle cells divide. What is this kind of growth called?
options: Hypertrophy
Atrophy
Angiogenesis
Hyperplasia

q: A soccer player's cast is removed after six weeks. His calf is visibly thinner than on the other leg. What has happened, and what is the outlook?
options: Disuse atrophy; it will reverse with use
Muscular dystrophy, which will slowly progress
Fibers were lost for good and replaced by scar tissue from fibroblasts
Hypertrophy of the fat under the skin

q: A deep cut severs the nerve to a man's forearm muscles, and the axons do not regrow. Compared with a forearm kept in a cast for the same time, how will his muscles change?
options: Milder atrophy than in the cast
About the same atrophy as in the cast
Hypertrophy as the fibers contract on their own
Worse atrophy, ending in replacement by fat and scar

q: Put the stages of skeletal muscle fiber formation in order.
options: Muscle stem cells commit to becoming muscle
Myoblasts divide and line up
Myoblasts fuse into a myotube with many nuclei
The myotube fills with myofibrils
Nuclei move to the edge of a mature fiber

q: A 4-year-old boy has trouble climbing stairs and pushes on his thighs with his hands to stand up. His calves look large and his blood creatine kinase is very high. What best explains the large calves?
options: Hypertrophy of normal fibers compensating for weakness
Fibers replaced by fat and connective tissue
Extra fibers made by hyperplasia
Swelling from lactate stored in the fibers

q: What triggers angiogenesis in muscle during endurance training?
options: VEGF released from working muscle low in oxygen
Lactate binding to receptor proteins on red blood cells in the muscle
Fast glycolytic fibers dividing into capillaries
Loss of the motor neuron supplying the muscle

q: Mr. Alvarez, 78, can still lift his grocery bags slowly, but he often stumbles and cannot catch himself in time. Which age-related change best explains his trouble catching himself?
options: His slow oxidative fibers have turned into fast glycolytic fibers
His muscle fibers have begun to divide abnormally
His muscles store more myoglobin, slowing them
His fast fibers have shrunk most, cutting his power

q: A student described how skeletal muscle repairs a small injury. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Muscle stem cells lying on the injured fiber's surface become active
The stem cells divide, and some daughters become myoblasts
The damaged mature fiber divides to replace its lost part
Myoblasts fuse with the damaged fiber, adding nuclei and patching it

q: You walk slowly across a room, then jump as high as you can. Which fibers in your calf muscles are active in each task?
options: Walking: fast glycolytic. Jumping: slow oxidative
Walking and jumping: all three types equally
Walking: mainly slow oxidative. Jumping: all three types
Walking: none. Jumping: fast glycolytic

q: Complete the order in which fiber types are recruited as the force a muscle must produce rises: slow oxidative → fast oxidative → ____.
options: Smooth muscle
Fast glycolytic
Slow oxidative again, at a higher rate
Cardiac muscle

q: Identical twins are separated at birth. One becomes a sprinter and the other an office worker. What would you predict about their thigh muscles as adults?
options: Very different proportions of slow and fast fibers, set by training
Similar slow-to-fast proportions, but different fiber size and aerobic capacity
Identical muscles in every respect, set by their genes
The sprinter's muscle will have twice as many fibers

q: In smooth muscle, which protein binds calcium and starts the chain of events leading to contraction?
options: Troponin
Calmodulin
Myoglobin
Tropomyosin

q: Put the steps of smooth muscle contraction in order.
options: Depolarization opens calcium channels in the sarcolemma
Calcium enters from the extracellular fluid
Calcium binds calmodulin
Calcium–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase
The kinase phosphorylates myosin heads
Myosin heads bind actin and cross-bridges cycle

q: Fill the gap: calcium binds calmodulin → ____ → myosin heads are phosphorylated → cross-bridges cycle.
options: Tropomyosin moves off actin's binding sites
Troponin changes shape
Myosin light-chain kinase is activated
Myosin phosphatase is activated

q: A student described smooth muscle contraction. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: A stimulus raises calcium in the cytosol, much of it from outside the cell
Calcium binds troponin on the thin filaments
Myosin light-chain kinase phosphorylates the myosin heads
Thin filaments pull the dense bodies closer together

q: An experimental drug blocks myosin light-chain kinase in the smooth muscle of a strip of intestine. The strip is then stimulated. Predict the change in each variable, compared with a strip without the drug.
The smooth muscle in artery walls stays partly contracted all day while using very little ATP. What explains this?
options: Its cross-bridges never detach, as in rigor mortis
It makes its ATP without using mitochondria at all
It stays in complete tetanus from constant nerve firing
Myosin heads held on as slowly cycling latch-bridges

q: Mrs. Dube takes a calcium channel blocker, a drug that blocks voltage-gated calcium channels in the smooth muscle of her arteries. Why does this widen her arteries?
options: Less calcium enters the fibers, so less binds calmodulin
The drug blocks troponin in the artery wall
The drug stops acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junctions of the arteries
More calcium is stored in the SR, which strengthens relaxation

q: As Mr. Yusuf's urinary bladder slowly fills from 50 mL to 400 mL over three hours, the pressure inside it barely rises. Which property of its smooth muscle explains this?
options: Tetanus of the bladder wall's smooth muscle
Stress-relaxation of the wall
Autorhythmicity of pacesetter cells
Rigor of the bladder's cross-bridges

q: The arrector pili muscles in your skin contract fiber by fiber when their nerve fibers signal them, and they rarely contract on their own. What kind of smooth muscle are they?
options: Single-unit smooth muscle
Multi-unit smooth muscle
Visceral smooth muscle
Cardiac muscle

q: A surgeon removes a short loop of intestine and places it in warm, oxygenated fluid, cut off from all nerves from the brain and spinal cord. Its wall keeps contracting in slow, regular, coordinated waves. What makes this possible?
options: Motor neurons inside the fluid stimulate each fiber separately
Each fiber contracts on its own, at its own random rhythm
Stored acetylcholine is released at neuromuscular junctions
Pacesetter waves spread by gap junctions

q: Select every feature of single-unit smooth muscle.
options: Fibers linked by many gap junctions
Spontaneous rhythmic activity from pacesetter cells
Each fiber controlled by its own nerve endings
Contraction in response to stretch
Found in the walls of the stomach, intestines and urinary bladder
Striations from lined-up sarcomeres

q: Compare the relaxed and contracted fibers. Why does the contracted fiber bulge and pucker instead of simply getting shorter?
options: Its sarcomeres shorten unevenly along the fiber
Filaments running diagonally pull the dense bodies together
The intermediate filaments contract and squeeze the cell
Water rushes into the cell each time it contracts

fig.alt: Two drawings of smooth muscle fibers. On the left, a relaxed fiber is long and spindle-shaped, crossed by a diagonal network of lines, the intermediate filaments, that join small dark dots, the dense bodies, spread through the cell and along its edge. On the right, a contracted fiber is shorter and wider, with a bulging, puckered outline, and arrows at both ends pointing inward; its dense bodies have been pulled closer together.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Intercalated disc
Dense body
Z disc
Sarcolemma

fig.alt: A small outline of the heart with a box on its wall, enlarged into a drawing of branching, striped cardiac muscle fibers beside a capillary. Each fiber has a central nucleus, and wavy intercalated discs join the fibers end to end. A further enlargement of one disc shows desmosomes holding the two membranes together and gap junctions bridging them.

q: Why can't cardiac muscle be driven into tetanus the way skeletal muscle can?
options: Cardiac muscle has no troponin on its thin filaments
Cardiac fibers are not linked by gap junctions
Its action potential lasts almost as long as its twitch
Cardiac muscle has no sarcoplasmic reticulum to store calcium

q: After a heart transplant, the donor heart has no nerve connections to the recipient's brain. Within minutes of restoring blood flow, it starts beating on its own. Which feature of cardiac muscle explains this?
options: Stress-relaxation
Autorhythmicity
Recruitment of motor units
Latch-bridges

q: Skeletal muscle grades its force by recruiting more motor units. How does the heart produce a stronger beat?
options: By recruiting fibers that were resting during the last beat
By summing beats into tetanus
More calcium released per beat
By switching its fibers over to anaerobic glycolysis

q: During a heart attack, blood flow to part of the heart wall stops. The muscle there stops contracting within about a minute and begins to die after 20 to 30 minutes, while resting skeletal muscle can survive a surgical tourniquet for an hour or more. Which feature best explains the difference?
options: Cardiac muscle has no myoglobin
Its near-total reliance on aerobic respiration
Cardiac muscle has no mitochondria
Its fibers are too thick for oxygen to diffuse into them

q: Smooth muscle can shorten further, and produce force over a wider range of lengths, than skeletal muscle. Which structural feature contributes to this?
options: Its sarcomeres are longer than those of skeletal muscle
Its Z discs are closer together
Myosin heads along each whole thick filament
It has more T tubules

q: Calcium in an artery's smooth muscle falls after a period of contraction, and myosin phosphatase removes phosphate from heads that are still attached to actin. Predict the change in each variable as the fiber enters the latch state.
A drug that blocks troponin would stop contraction in which muscle types?
options: Smooth muscle alone
Skeletal and smooth muscle
Cardiac and smooth muscle
Skeletal and cardiac muscle
misconception: all muscle is switched on by calcium binding troponin
